articles.title: Capturing the media/cultural imperialism debate: Latin American and Anglophone views in perspective
articles.abstract: The debate on cultural imperialism flourished in the 1960s and the 1970s, closely tied to the process of decolonization, which gained ground in the decades following World War 2. In the 1960s and 1970s, Latin America became a particularly important hub to this debate. This changed, however. By the 1990s, a group of Anglophone scholars—most of them working from the very same countries (US and UK) pointed to as the main agents of cultural imperialism in the world—came to dominate the debate on this topic. This article intends to discuss how the academic Anglosphere captured the debate on media/cultural imperialism, what consequences followed, and what are the prospects for this topic in a new, emerging multipolar world order.

articles.title: Monsters, magic, mediality: Tabletop role–playing games as mediatization processes
articles.authors: Lukas Daniel Klausner, Tobias Unterhuber, Franziska Ascher
articles.abstract: Tabletop role-playing games (TTRPGs) are often thought of as an analog medium. But their recent renaissance (fueled by the emergence of actual plays and the subsequent increase of online game sessions due to the COVID-19 pandemic) shows how entangled TTRPGs are and have been with the process of digitalization – and that they are better understood as a hybrid medium in general. Understanding TTRPGs this way leads, in turn, to the understanding of role-playing as a cluster of mediatization processes between its different parts, be it players and game masters, narrative and rules, or even reality and fiction. This paper thus analyzes TTRPGs’ mediality and its relationship to other media (computer (games), boardgames, actual plays and the role of the players) to bring various academic disciplines and different branches of game studies into dialogue with one another through the focus on TTRPGs.

articles.title: Prompting with Respect: Cultural Norms and User Experience in LLM Interactions
articles.authors: Sujin Yang, Seoyoung Oh, Ha Eun Shim
articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in prompt engineering, its influence on user experience—particularly in relation to cultural communication norms—remains largely unexplored. This controlled experiment examined how respectful versus directive prompting—a culturally meaningful contrast in Korean—affects Korean users’ psychological experience during LLM interactions. Forty-three Korean female college students were randomly assigned to respectful prompt (RP) (using polite requests, compliments, and gratitude) or directive prompt (DP) (using imperatives, criticism, and performance-based penalties) conditions. Participants completed a writing task using ChatGPT. Results indicated that RPs yielded significantly higher satisfaction, particularly for affinity and likability, whereas the difference in perceived output quality was smaller and nonsignificant. Furthermore, RPs elicited socially supportive ChatGPT responses, whereas DPs were followed by apologies, suggesting bidirectional social adaptation between users and ChatGPT. Together, these findings suggest that culturally grounded communicative conventions may shape users’ subjective experience even where perceived output quality does not differ significantly, pointing to culturally adaptive large language model systems that recognize diverse communication patterns as essential design considerations rather than imposing universal paradigms.

Antecedents and consequences of face filter use on social media: the role of use frequency and depth
articles.authors: Jingjing Tong, Chunyi Xian, Jingjun (David) Xu
articles.abstract: Purpose Face filters are pervasive in selfie-based social media practices, raising concerns about their psychological implications. This study examines the social drivers of face-filter use frequency and depth, their positive and negative psychological consequences and how these two dimensions jointly shape user outcomes. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on self-discrepancy theory (SDT), we conceptualize descriptive and subjective norms as self-guides influencing two dimensions of filter use: frequency (which regulates discrepancy accessibility) and depth (which regulates discrepancy availability). We propose a model linking filter use to affective outcomes and self-evaluations and examine the interactive effects of use frequency and depth on these outcomes. The model was tested using survey data from 328 participants. Findings Descriptive and subjective norms positively predict use frequency and depth. Use frequency, but not use depth, increases self-confidence by enhancing appearance self-esteem; whereas both frequency and depth increase negative moods by amplifying self-discrepancy perceptions. Additionally, the interaction between use frequency and depth is positively associated with both appearance self-esteem and perceived self-discrepancy. Originality/value This study is among the first to integrate SDT and social norms to explain the antecedents and dual consequences of face-filter use. By distinguishing use frequency and depth as two self-regulation dimensions in digital self-presentation, this study highlights their main and interactive effects on positive and negative psychological outcomes and clarifies the underlying mechanisms.

articles.title: Improving fintech services through human–machine interactions: user anthropomorphic perception through an affordance lens
articles.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how technology features influence anthropomorphic perceptions among users, focusing on interactive technology such as interactive voice response (IVR). By employing a sociotechnical framework, the study emphasises the role of design affordances in fostering human-like qualities in digital systems, particularly within financial services contexts. Design/methodology/approach Using a case study methodology, the research examines IVR technology deployed to financial savings clients at a Ghanaian savings and loans institution. Data were collected through user interactions and analysed through an affordance lens to identify key design elements that evoke anthropomorphic perceptions. Findings The study identifies ways in which the IVR system evoked human-like qualities. These were shaped by design affordances, including personalised voice messages, culturally relevant content and a consistent human-like persona. The findings reveal how user emotions and imagination mediate anthropomorphic perceptions in digital system interactions. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to a single case in a specific cultural and financial context, which may affect generalisability. Future research should explore diverse contexts and technologies to validate the findings and expand understanding of anthropomorphic design. Practical implications Insights from this study inform the design of culturally attuned and user-friendly digital systems. By leveraging anthropomorphic features, financial services can foster greater trust, engagement and user satisfaction in their technology solutions. Social implications Anthropomorphic design can improve access to financial services, especially for underbanked populations, by enhancing usability and trust in digital platforms. This approach also supports inclusive technology design that respects cultural nuances. Originality/value This study offers a novel sociotechnical perspective on anthropomorphism in Information Systems research, demonstrating how design affordances evoke human-like perceptions. It provides actionable guidance for designing engaging and culturally relevant digital systems in financial services.

articles.title: Promotion or substitution? The effect of AI assistants on physician performance in online healthcare platforms
articles.authors: Weicheng Wang, Shaoqi Zhang, Min Zhang, Xitong Guo
articles.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping healthcare delivery. Physician-specific AI assistants, trained on individual physicians’ medical data, now provide personalized medical advice on online healthcare platforms. While AI assistants improve the availability of physician expertise, they may substitute for cognitive tasks traditionally undertaken by physicians. Despite this tension, few studies have examined how AI assistants affect physician performance. This study aims to examine the causal impact of introducing AI assistants on physician consultation volume and how physicians’ existing resource configurations shape this impact. Design/methodology/approach This study leveraged the introduction of AI assistants on a leading online healthcare platform to establish a quasi-natural experimental setting. We constructed a panel dataset covering 3,668 physicians and employed a difference-in-differences model to identify the causal effect of AI assistants on physician performance. Findings The results suggest that the introduction of AI assistants significantly improves physician performance, with physicians experiencing a 3.6% increase in consultation volume. Moderation analyses reveal that the positive effect is weaker for high-reputation physicians and those with broader knowledge. Further heterogeneity analysis shows that the effect is invariant to physician gender but more pronounced among physicians in non-first-tier cities. Originality/value This study provides causal evidence of the impact of AI assistants on individual performance in an online healthcare setting. It further reveals how physicians’ existing resource configurations shape AI’s impact from a resource-based view and offers suggestive evidence on its promotion and substitution pathways.

articles.title: The impact of algorithmic control on app-workers’ counterproductive work behavior: from an objectification perspective
articles.authors: Ming Chi, Yanli Chen, Yongshun Xu, Yuetong Wu, Yihao Yang
articles.abstract: Purpose Drawing on the stressor-strain-outcome model and an objectification perspective, this study examines how algorithmic control is associated with app-workers’ counterproductive work behavior through organizational objectification and self-objectification. It further investigates perceived algorithmic transparency as a boundary condition. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 498 DiDi Chuxing drivers in China through a three-wave survey. The measurement model was assessed using SmartPLS 4, while ordinary least squares regression and conditional process analysis in SPSS 27.0 were used to test the direct, indirect, serial mediation, and moderation effects. Findings Algorithmic control was positively associated with counterproductive work behavior through organizational objectification and self-objectification, both separately and sequentially. Perceived algorithmic transparency weakened the positive relationships between algorithmic control and both forms of objectification. Practical implications Algorithmic governance may backfire when workers perceive that they are being treated as instruments or begin to evaluate themselves in instrumental terms. Platforms should reduce instrumental treatment in evaluation and enforcement, provide explanatory feedback, and use targeted transparency to support workers’ understanding of algorithmic decisions. Originality/value This study identifies a sequential objectification mechanism linking algorithmic control to counterproductive work behavior and demonstrates how perceived algorithmic transparency conditions this process.

articles.title: Reducing supply chain uncertainty via blockchain: an affordance and transaction cost perspective
articles.authors: Wilson K.S. Leung, Man Kit Chang, Man Lai Cheung, Si Shi, Randy Yee Man Wong
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines how blockchain technology supports uncertainty reduction and collaboration in supply chains, thereby improving perceived business process performance. Drawing on affordance theory and transaction cost theory, we investigate how transparency and traceability affordances reduce environmental and partner-related uncertainties and facilitate supply chain collaboration. Design/methodology/approach We collected data from 297 supply chain managers in China. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to test the proposed relationships among blockchain affordances, uncertainty reduction, collaboration and performance outcomes. Findings The results show that the traceability affordance significantly reduces all types of uncertainty, while the transparency affordance indirectly contributes to uncertainty reduction through traceability. Reduced uncertainty strengthens supply chain collaboration, which in turn improves perceived business process performance. Research limitations/implications This study identifies uncertainty reduction as a key mechanism linking blockchain affordances to supply chain collaboration and perceived business process performance. As the study focuses primarily on uncertainty within transaction cost theory, future research could examine other transaction characteristics and contextual conditions that shape blockchain affordances and their consequences. Practical implications Managers should establish supply chain transparency while prioritizing traceability for high-risk products and suppliers. Blockchain-enabled audit trails can support supplier evaluation, transaction verification and contract monitoring, providing a stronger informational basis for interorganizational collaboration. Originality/value This study explains how blockchain affordances translate into collaborative and performance outcomes through uncertainty reduction. The findings further distinguish the roles of transparency and traceability in this process, providing a more nuanced understanding of how blockchain creates value in supply chain relationships.

articles.title: Adult Children’s Chronic Health Conditions and Intergenerational Financial Transfers Between Parents and Early Midlife Adult Children: Variation Across Sons and Daughters
articles.abstract: As our population ages, adult children and parents will experience greater overlap across their lives, offering more opportunities to engage in intergenerational financial transfers. Intergenerational transfers benefit both generations. They may be especially crucial as parents encounter challenges associated with aging, and as adult children grapple with their own health problems. We used the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health data to explore whether an adult child’s chronic health conditions in young adulthood were associated with financial transfers between early midlife adult children and their parents, factoring in differences between sons and daughters. More specifically, we examined the dynamics of upward, downward, and mutual financial transfers among adult children reporting no chronic conditions, one chronic condition, two chronic conditions (multimorbidity), or three or more chronic conditions (severe multimorbidity). Our results indicate adult children with severe multimorbidity were more likely than adult children without chronic health conditions to receive downward financial transfers from their parents. Moreover, adult children with multimorbidity were more likely than adult children without chronic health conditions to engage in mutual financial transfers. Regarding gender of the adult child, we found among children reporting one chronic condition, sons were less likely to engage in downward, upward, and mutual transfers with parents relative to daughters. This research advances our understanding of how an adult child’s chronic health conditions shape dynamics of financial transfers with parents.

articles.title: Seeing I to I Makes Sparks Fly: Daily Diary Investigation of I-Sharing and Relationship Quality
articles.authors: Rachael M. Cavallaro, Tiffany George, Grace N. Rivera
articles.abstract: I-sharing (i.e., the perception that one shares the same subjective experience) with a romantic partner positively predicts relationship satisfaction and perceptions that one’s partner knows one’s true self (i.e., perceived partner true self knowledge. The current work extends the research on I-sharing in romantic relationships by investigating whether daily fluctuations in perceptions of I-sharing with a romantic partner positively relate to daily romantic relationship outcomes such as relationship quality (i.e., relationship flourishing and satisfaction), perceived partner true self knowledge (PTSK), and perceived compassionate acts towards one’s romantic partner. The current work also investigates whether these relationships are independent of Me-sharing (e.g., perceiving one has similar personality traits with one’s partner). The study included a cross-sectional intake survey ( N = 204), followed by a daily diary component ( N = 162, K = 850). Perceived I-sharing frequency does have positive relationships with all the aforementioned romantic relationship outcomes, independent of Me-sharing. These results suggest that daily perceptions of I-sharing frequency are positively associated with several distinct daily aspects of people’s romantic relationships, such as the satisfaction and the sense of fulfillment people derive from a romantic relationship.

articles.title: Extra-Familial Intergenerational Contact in the Contemporary United States: Exploring Its Frequency, Nature, and Correlates
articles.abstract: Some major studies conducted over the last forty years suggest that intergenerational contact between younger and older adults (i.e., those aged 70+) in Western contexts is scarce. However, the phrasing of questions asked in these studies leaves open the possibility that intergenerational contact might not be so rare. In Study 1 ( n = 399), we surveyed young Americans about the frequency and characteristics of their intergenerational interactions. In Study 2 ( n = 278), we surveyed a separate sample of young Americans to assess the quantity and communicative quality of their contact with older people, gather information about their intergenerational relationships, and gauge their attitudes towards aging. In Study 1, 42% of respondents had at least one friend aged 70 or older and over 60% had had contact (typically face-to-face) with an older adult during the previous week. In Study 2, the quality and quantity of contact were associated with the endorsement of prescriptive age-based stereotypes, both directly and indirectly via perceptions of common ingroup identity. Moreover, quantity and quality of contact predicted the affective responses younger adults had at the thought of growing old, and their sense of efficacy about doing so. Our results suggest that the state of intergenerational relations in the United States is less dire than some might believe, and that high-quality contact with older adults is associated not only with less negative stereotypes but also younger people feeling both less troubled by and better able to cope with their own aging.

articles.title: Economic Conditions, Public Sentiment, and News Coverage: A Time-Series Analysis of Economic Agenda Dynamics in South Korea
articles.abstract: Drawing on 23 years of economic news in South Korea, this study investigates how key economic indicators interact with the volume and tone of economic news, which can both shape and reflect public opinion, particularly the public’s economic sentiment. Time-series analyses revealed that unfavorable economic conditions, reflected in lower Stock Market Index and GDP growth rates as well as higher Consumer Price Index (CPI) and unemployment rates, were associated with greater news coverage of these topics in the subsequent month. The tone of news coverage was largely unrelated to economic indicators, suggesting that the overall news sentiment may not closely align with real-world economic conditions. Finally, the relationship between economic news and public sentiment was reciprocal rather than one-directional. Implications for economic journalism are discussed in detail.

articles.title: Online Political Harassment Targeting German and Swedish Trans Advocates: Does Platform Governance Make a Difference?
articles.abstract: Online platforms are crucial for political activists worldwide, but platform affordances also enable harassment and silencing of marginalized groups. Platform regulations are one of the main ways to curb hateful attacks, and democratic states are increasingly adopting legislation that targets big tech companies, including their content moderation. Focusing on the polarized 2024 debates around new gender self-identification laws in Sweden and Germany, this study explores how trans advocates experience online political harassment, with particular attention to their exposure to and the impacts of such attacks, and whether national platform regulations, such as the German NetzDG, shape these experiences. Drawing on interviews with leading LGBTIQ+ advocates, the findings suggest that such regulations make little difference in practice. Advocates in both Sweden and Germany reported unprecedented levels of harassment on social media during the debates, with significant consequences for their mental health and continued political engagement. The impact was particularly severe for advocates with intersecting marginalized identities, who often lacked institutional support and were targeted personally for being trans. Respondents also noted increased attacks from trans-exclusionary feminists, underscoring the need for closer scrutiny of these actors in countries regarded as frontrunners in gender equality and LGBTIQ+ rights protection.

articles.title: Dynamics of (In)Visibility: Immanent Potential of Young Feminism Across and Beneath the Square
articles.authors: Danbi Kim, Miran Pyun, Yeran Kim
articles.abstract: The invisibilization of feminist activism driven by postfeminist trends and the strategic use of invisibility to build safe communities free from oppression represent two sides of the same coin. Both treat invisibility as a passively determined stage preceding visible activism. Moving beyond this understanding, the current study explores the immanent potential of invisibility within contemporary feminist activism by conceptualizing (in)visibility through Deleuze’s conceptual pair of the virtual and the actual. In Deleuze’s philosophy, the virtual is the immaterial potential that constitutes reality, whereas the actual is the materialization of virtuality into a specific form through the process of actualization. Accordingly, we conceptualize invisibility as a persistent potential that exerts power across and beneath the surface and enables visibilization of activism upon encountering a specific event. Drawing on interviews with 20 women aged 22–35 who participated in the 2024–2025 anti-martial law protests in South Korea, this study examines how the potential of invisibility is actualized as activism. We analyze three interrelated dimensions: the temporality through which women cultivated their inherent potential while being politically and socially invisibilized; the virtual spatiality that mediates invisibility and visibility, enabling the actualization of that potential; and the physical spatiality in which activism is materialized as an inclusive and distinctive protest culture. Through this approach, we seek to uncover the dynamic potential immanent in invisible forms and fundamentally rethink the relationship between invisibility and visibility in activism.

articles.title: Resisting the Boys’ Club: Tactical Agency, Gendered Performances, and Professional Survival in Czech Political Journalism
articles.authors: Iveta Jansová, Marína Urbániková, Lenka Waschková Císařová
articles.abstract: In the still masculinized “boys’ club” of political journalism, women are frequently cast as passive subjects of systemic exclusion. This article subverts that narrative, moving beyond traditional victim-centric frameworks to explore the granular, everyday navigation of female and male journalists within gendered professional structures. Leveraging a robust longitudinal dataset of 139 interviews across three iterative waves, we reveal how and why political journalists deploy complex strategies and tactics to secure professional survival and visibility. This approach demonstrates how specific situational triggers fluidly shape these choices in daily practice. Ultimately, this study highlights the profound ambivalence of individual agency: While these highly restricted tactical choices enable daily survival within a hostile reporting environment, they temporarily accommodate, rather than dismantle, the underlying status quo, directly underscoring an urgent need for institutional and structural evolution.

articles.title: Smartphone-Based GenAI and the Ruralization of Indian-Language News
articles.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of smartphone-based generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on the editing and increasing representation of rural news in Hindi-language speed news in India. As an innovation, speed news refers to the recitation of news summaries by presenters at an accelerated pace across mobile, television, and digital platforms such as YouTube. Drawing on the anthropological conception of “ruralization” and fieldwork in northern India, I argue that smartphone-based GenAI enables small, rural actors working mainly with mobile phones to more effectively condense and edit speed news stories. Smartphone-based GenAI tools such as ChatGPT help package raw speed news stories into pithy, punchy sentences that resemble a form of kahawat (“saying”) or sutra (“aphorism”), thereby striking cultural chords with Hindi-language news audiences, particularly in rural India. This improved news-editing process also facilitates the steady production of speed news bulletins, contributing to the deeper ruralization of Hindi news. The commentary concludes with a brief reflection on the potentials and pitfalls of smartphone-based GenAI in India.

articles.title: Building Deep Data Through Screens: Princeton-SMART for Mobile Communication Research
articles.authors: Jihye Lee, Kentaro Oriuchi, Daniel Muise, Jacob N. Shapiro
articles.abstract: This article introduces Princeton-SMART, open-source screen-capture software designed to generate deep data on mobile communication behavior. Princeton-SMART unobtrusively collects screenshots and on-screen text from Android devices at short intervals in naturalistic settings. We describe a research pipeline for secure data collection, preprocessing, and analysis, drawing on over 1.5 million screenshots contributed by U.S. job seekers over 6 weeks. We demonstrate how job-search activities can be identified using vision-language AI models and methodological considerations encountered during the process. We conclude by discussing opportunities and practical implications for integrating Princeton-SMART into mobile communication research.

articles.title: “ In a way, I want TikTok to tell me what I want. . . ” Users’ experience of TikTok as a televisual algorithmic flow
articles.authors: Carlos Entrena-Serrano, Trisha Meyer, Emilia Gómez, Jo Pierson
articles.abstract: This article revisits Williams’s concept of flow, Firth’s notion of algorithmic flow, and Picone et al.’s concept of Small Acts of Engagement (SAOE) to examine how users experience TikTok’s algorithmic flow. SAOE are understood as low-effort, everyday acts through which users negotiate their identities and shape their digital consumption. While SAOE have been a valuable lens for understanding user agency on earlier social media platforms, we argue that TikTok’s interface design and cultural framing introduce new challenges. The platform’s design, together with users’ perception of TikTok’s algorithmic flow as a televisual experience, reduces their SAOE to a minimal expression: a rhythm of watch, scroll, repeat , discouraging other forms of intentional, identity-driven engagement. Through a mixed-methods study combining interviews and analysis of participants’ donated TikTok data, we show how our participants experience TikTok as a place for effortless entertainment and continuous consumption, closely resembling the experience of traditional television flow.

Commercial entanglements and online visibility: University priorities and the making of scientific legitimacy
articles.abstract: Universities in many parts of the world now encourage faculty to patent inventions, launch start-ups, and promote their work via online platforms. Through commercialization support and the inclusion of social media metrics in tenure reviews, they have cultivated forms of scientific life oriented toward market ties and Internet visibility. Technology transfer offices support the development of discoveries from academic labs into faculty-led ventures and (often exclusive) licensing partnerships—as in the case of epigenetic age tests examined here. The paper traces how these research tools were transformed into consumer products promoted on social media by researchers at elite US universities. In doing so, it shows how university policies and programs enable forms of scientific authority rooted in public performance and market traction. These developments are reshaping academic legitimacy, as forms of authority most easily amplified online gain institutional validation through engagement and impact metrics—often promoting charismatic, entrepreneurial, gendered performances of expertise.

articles.title: Communicating scientific uncertainty: Exploring science journalists’ understandings, challenges, and strategies
articles.authors: Finja Isabel Augsburg, Fabian Prochazka, Eva Thomm, Johannes Bauer
articles.abstract: Science journalists are central intermediaries in communicating the uncertainties of science to the public. Socio-scientific issues like COVID-19 and climate change highlight the importance of addressing uncertainties to support informed decision-making while underscoring the complexities involved. Based on 13 semi-structured interviews with science journalists, this study links their conceptual understanding of scientific uncertainty to the strategies and challenges they face in communicating it. Results suggest that journalists primarily see uncertainty as the inability of science to provide simple answers to complex questions due to limited or conflicting evidence. They emphasize uncertainty’s dual role: it helps explain how science generates knowledge and fosters trust when communicated effectively, yet it also causes confusion, frustration, and loss of trust if communicated poorly. Maintaining trust in science and journalism thus emerges as the meta-challenge in reporting uncertainty, for which journalists describe nine strategies, including contextualizing uncertainty and prioritizing realistic assessments over amplifying controversy.

articles.title: Understanding the Effects of Message Complexity and Epistemic Uncertainty on Attitudinal, Cognitive, and Behavioral Responses to Messages About Microplastics
articles.abstract: This study examined how message complexity and epistemic uncertainty affect attitudes toward science, information overload, and behavioral intention using a 2 × 2 factorial design. Although no main effects were detected, the interaction between complexity and uncertainty on information overload depended on intolerance of uncertainty (IU): uncertainty reduced information overload for low-IU individuals but increased it for high-IU individuals. Moreover, the conditional indirect effect of uncertainty on behavioral intention through information overload was significant under high message complexity at specific levels of IU. When message complexity was low, this indirect effect was not significant at any level of IU.

articles.title: The Effects of Online Harassment of Scientists on Bystander Scientists
articles.authors: Jana Laura Egelhofer, Christina Seeger, Alice Binder
articles.abstract: Scientists who share research on social media increasingly face harassment, which is visible to many bystanders, including other scientists. We report a preregistered experiment testing how exposure to such harassment affects bystander scientists ( N = 846). Drawing on social identity approaches, we argue that bystander scientists may react similarly to directly targeted scientists. Results show that exposure to harassment increases anxiety and risk perceptions but does not reduce willingness to engage in science communication; it slightly increases perceived trustworthiness of targeted scientists. Presumed influence shapes some of these effects. Shifting attention to bystanders, we highlight broader societal consequences of harassment against scientists.

articles.title: Visibility, Sovereignty, and the Affective Politics of Media: Decolonial Struggles Over Representation and Reception During the 2022 Indigenous Protests in Ecuador
articles.abstract: This article examines how visibility, affect, and epistemic power intersected during the June 2022 Indigenous-led protests in Ecuador, when media became a central terrain of struggle over meaning and legitimacy. Combining multimodal media analysis with ethnographically informed audience research, the study compares three communicative regimes: government, commercial, and Indigenous/community media, to show how each enacted distinct infrastructures of visibility and political intelligibility. Government media constructed visibility as surveillance, framing dissent as a crisis of order through securitized language, ritualized imagery, and affective scripts that moved audiences from fear to reassurance. Commercial broadcasters pursued legitimacy through moderation, translating protest into economic disruption and containing conflict through the aesthetics of balance and procedural neutrality. In contrast, Indigenous/community media operating through platformed livestreams enacted visibility as relational sovereignty, embedding communication within collective action, historical continuity, and participatory verification. Drawing on decolonial media theory and scholarship on affective publics and Indigenous digital activism, the article conceptualizes media as ontopolitical infrastructures that organize not only information but the conditions under which political subjects and truths become recognizable. Reception data from Kichwa-speaking communities demonstrate that Indigenous audiences engaged in collective practices of interpretation, verification, and refusal. Affective responses such as anger and pride functioned as epistemic resources, transforming exposure into critique and reception into communal knowledge-making. The article advances a decolonial reframing of visibility as infrastructure and theorizes reception as epistemic labor sustaining narrative sovereignty.

articles.title: It Doesn’t Take Extremes to Trigger Hate: A Mixed-Methods Study on Meme Extremity and User Comments on 9GAG
articles.abstract: Users engage with socially and politically relevant topics by sharing memes and adopting the creative styles of meme-sharing platforms like 9GAG. Although memes can contain political critique, research also linked them to hate speech and increasingly extreme content. Little attention has been paid to entertainment-first platforms, where (perceived) homogeneity, anonymity, and humor-driven social norms may shape how political and hateful content is produced and discussed in the comment section. This study addresses this gap using a sequential mixed-methods design. First, we analyzed 343 memes on 9GAG with quantitative content analysis, categorizing them into classes based on varying degrees of extreme content using latent class analysis. Second, via qualitative content analysis, we investigated the comment sections of six memes representing each identified class to determine how extreme content levels influence hateful comments. Results show that anonymity and ingroup identity foster a climate in which hate is normalized and often obscured through humor. However, even purely humorous memes provoked hateful comments, suggesting that factors beyond meme extremity, like topic sensitivity and referenced outgroups, also shape hateful follow-up communication.

articles.title: How Definitions Shape Our Understanding of Political Influencers on Social Media
articles.authors: Jennifer Oser, John Wagner, Nir Grinberg
articles.abstract: Political discourse now circulates through sprawling social media networks where multiple actors wield influence in addition to traditional elites. Yet scholarly conclusions about who actually shapes that discourse diverge because leading studies operationalize “political influencer” in fundamentally different ways. To clarify the stakes of those choices—and advance more coherent theorizing—we examine six definitions that are prevalent in the literature and are rooted in audience size, elite ties, network importance, and message engagement. We then apply these distinctive definitions to a single dataset, namely a panel of 597,815 registered U.S. voters on Twitter during the 2020 presidential campaign to identify convergence and divergence across definitions. Three patterns emerge. First, conceptual boundaries matter: definitions that differ in scale rarely converge on the same influencers, confirming that different lenses reveal largely distinct influencer groups. Second, definitional emphasis reshapes the portrait of influence itself: elite-based criteria surface highly political, centrally positioned senders with compact but engaged followings, whereas follower- and engagement-based criteria net vastly larger, more heterogeneous groups that address politics only episodically. Third, upstream choices about conceptual boundaries and definitional emphases cascade downstream to the characteristics of influencers’ audiences, producing systematic shifts in followers’ age, gender, racial, and partisan characteristics. By showing how conceptual decisions impact both who counts as a political influencer and which citizens follow their messages, this study lays the groundwork for clearer conceptualization of the relevant dimensions for advancing the accumulation of knowledge on this increasingly important political phenomenon.

articles.title: Modeling Civic Engagement in the Age of AI: A Communication Mediation Approach to AI News, Multifaceted Trust, and Participation in a Two-Wave Panel Study
articles.authors: Seungahn Nah, Fanjue Liu, Jun Luo, Lee LaPlaca, Chris DeFelice
articles.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes both a topic of news coverage and a force shaping the information environment, citizens must make sense of AI-related issues while evaluating machine-generated content, journalistic coverage, and institutional actors. This study applies the Orientation-Stimulus-Reasoning-Orientation-Response framework to examine how AI-related news consumption is associated with interpersonal discussion, multifaceted trust, and AI-related offline civic participation. Using two-wave panel data from U.S. adults (Wave 1 = 2,010; Wave 2 = 942), the study models AI-related news consumption across television, newspapers, online news sites, and social media as the stimulus; AI-related online and offline discussion as reasoning; trust in AI-generated news, legacy media coverage of AI, and AI-related institutional actors as reorientation; and AI-related offline civic participation as the response. Results reveal a selective communication pathway. Newspaper and social media AI news use were the most consistent predictors of AI-related discussion. Online discussion was associated with later trust in AI-generated news and legacy media coverage of AI, and trust in AI-generated news and AI-related institutional actors was associated with later offline participation. The observed indirect pathways operated through online discussion and trust in AI-generated news. These findings refine communication mediation research by showing that public engagement with AI-related issues depends on where people encounter AI news, how they discuss it, and which sources and institutions they come to trust.

articles.title: Eating the Stars: The Iconic Path of Eta Carinae and its Homunculus Nebula
articles.abstract: This visual essay is an experiment based on the life of astronomical images. It revolves around the notion of the ‘iconic path’ and discusses the way celestial light transmutes into different visual representations, thus acquiring new meanings, shapes and functions. This exceptional journey departs from the light of the Eta Carinae star and its Homunculus Nebula and ends up in our stomach. The essay is based upon the idea that pictures do not simply ‘illustrate’ the external world, but are the actual materials used to produce arguments about outer space. The familiarity of celestial objects depends enormously on how the astronomical data (i.e. the light received by technological artifacts) is translated into forms that are familiar to human vision and cognition. In short, we mainly know the universe as an image. We would like to take you on a journey to see how the Eta Carinae star and its Homunculus Nebula migrate from one picture to another. Each visual form that we discuss is situated within what we call ‘a territory’. In this text, we distinguish between scientific territories, artistic territories, consumption territories, public dissemination territories and even ‘bodily territories’ where our stomach belongs. The iconic path of the images of Eta Carinae and its Homunculus Nebula starts in the scientific territories, continues in the artistic and public ones, and finishes in our body. The reason for establishing this iconic path within the territories of science and aesthetics is that ‘Astronomical images exist at an intersection of science and art, of information and aesthetics, of the contextual and the visual’ (Smith et al., 2015, ‘Is that real? Understanding astronomical images’, in Journal of Media and Communication Studies 7[5]: 89). Finally, the iconic path proposed in this work is amalgamated to form the constellation of pictures as a final destination of this iconic path.

articles.title: Multimodal art–science ensembles: tracking the shift from a scientific data graph into wearable hand-loomed beadwork
articles.abstract: This article investigates what happens when a two-dimensional scientific data visualization is translated into a tactile, wearable object, and how that translation alters the meaning-making potential of science communication. The authors present a case study in which a genetic admixture chart mapping the diversity of African populations is transformed into hand-loomed beadwork by the Marigold cooperative (Bulawayo, Zimbabwe), in collaboration with scientists at the Sydney Brenner Institute for Molecular Bioscience (Wits University, South Africa). Using a multimodal and transmodal framework with a focus on touch, tangibility and materiality, the article tracks sequential shifts from PDF chart to pixellated pattern to beadwork, and finally to exhibition ensembles that orchestrate visual, spatial and linguistic modes. The authors argue that the hand-made, bodily and social presence embedded in beadwork provides new perspectives on connections between data and people, contributing to engagement with both science and art. The ensembles further mediate access by enabling different entry points, enriching interpretation. They show how these modal transitions modulate genre and affect, thickening the communicative affordances of the original scientific visualization, and in turn the meaning-potential of the beadwork.
